title: Promise and Pitfalls of Practitioner 'Action' Research, Part 3
author: Firth, Jonathan
summary: The final part of a three-part series, this piece weighs the genuine promise of teacher-led 'action research' against its real methodological and ethical pitfalls, arriving at a measured set of guardrails rather than a simple endorsement or dismissal. On the promise side, the author argues practitioner-researchers have advantages an outside researcher can't replicate: students behave normally around a teacher they already know, the teacher can identify exactly which curriculum content suits a given evidence-based technique, and they can track a class over days or weeks in a way external researchers rarely can. On the pitfall side, he's blunt about the risks — research on students without ethics training, findings that are hard to interpret without statistical expertise (especially with small samples), and a tendency for teachers to chase fun or fashionable ideas rather than the areas where evidence is already strongest, all compounded by institutional pressure to publicize findings that amplifies any errors. His concrete guidance reframes the goal of early practitioner research away from producing shareable 'findings' and toward building the practitioner's own methodological awareness, with ethical oversight handled institutionally rather than left to the individual, and internal sharing treated as critique-focused rather than as validation.
points: Names the practitioner-researcher's real advantages precisely: normal student behavior around a familiar teacher, curriculum-specific insight into where to apply a technique, and the ability to track a class over weeks.

Names the real risks just as precisely: no ethics training when researching on one's own students, findings that are hard to interpret without statistics expertise in small samples, and chasing fashionable ideas over evidence-backed ones.
Recommends ethical oversight be handled by an institutional ethics board, not left to the individual teacher-researcher's own judgment.
Reframes the goal for early-career practitioner research: the value is the practitioner's own increased methodological awareness, not necessarily shareable 'findings.'
quotes: One is ethical – without experience and ethics guidance, there are problems with carrying out research on students. Another is methodological, with a key issue being that findings are hard to interpret without methodology and statistics expertise.
The classroom practitioner knows their students, meaning that students are more likely to act in a normal way. With an external investigator their behaviour may not reflect the norm.
There is also a risk that teachers focus only on what seems fun or fashionable, ignoring the most impactful areas where there is already a body of theory and evidence.
Ethical choices are best not left up to the individual practitioner-researcher. Organisations that do not already have ethics boards for oversight should establish these.

At least to start with, the most important learning that occurs from practitioner research involves the increased awareness on the part of the practitioner, rather than 'research findings' that can be shared.
